nameStory: The bog copper gets its name from its beautiful copper-colored wings and its exclusive home in acidic bogs. Sometimes called the cranberry-bog copper, this butterfly has such a tight relationship with cranberry plants that it literally never leaves the bog where it was born!
description: The bog copper is a small butterfly with shimmery copper-orange wings that gleam in the sunlight. Like other members of the gossamer-winged butterfly family, it has delicate, almost translucent wings that seem to shimmer as it flies. These butterflies have a weak, fluttering flight pattern and stay very close to the ground as they move around their boggy homes. They're quite small, making them easy to overlook as they flutter among the low cranberry plants.

idTips.label: Copper-colored wings
idTips.description: Wings have a distinctive metallic copper-orange sheen that catches the light like a new penny

idTips.label: Weak, low flight
idTips.description: Flies with a fluttering, weak pattern very close to the ground, rarely rising above knee height

idTips.label: Bog habitat exclusive
idTips.description: Found only in acidic bogs with cranberry plants - if you're not in a squishy, wet bog, it's not a bog copper

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Tiny butterfly that's easy to miss, with gossamer-thin wings that seem almost transparent at the edges

idTips.label: Cranberry association
idTips.description: Always seen near cranberry plants, often sipping nectar from the small pink bell-shaped flowers

habitat: Bog coppers live exclusively in acidic bogs and wetlands where cranberries grow wild. These sphagnum moss-dominated areas have that characteristic squishy, bouncy feeling underfoot and smell faintly acidic. You'll find them in places like kettle hole bogs, cranberry bogs, and acidic fens throughout New England's glacially-carved landscape.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not typically active in spring, as most of their life is spent as eggs through the winter months.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time when adults emerge and can be seen nectaring on cranberry flowers and sipping dewdrops from leaves in early morning.
seasonality.fall: Flight period may extend into early fall, with mating and egg-laying occurring on cranberry plants before winter.
seasonality.winter: Exists entirely as eggs attached to cranberry plants, spending 85% of their entire lifespan in this dormant stage.

funFact: This butterfly spends an incredible 85% of its entire life as an egg - imagine being in kindergarten for most of your existence, then suddenly becoming an adult for just a few weeks!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small copper butterflies, but habitat is the key - bog coppers are the only copper butterfly that lives exclusively in acidic bogs. If you're standing on solid, dry ground, you're not looking at a bog copper!
contextualKnowledge: The bog copper is listed as a species of special concern in Connecticut due to habitat loss, as many bogs have been drained or developed. Their extreme habitat specialization makes them vulnerable to even small changes in their wetland homes.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives the Bronze Copper and Dorcas Copper, the bog copper is strictly limited to acidic bog habitats and never ventures into meadows, fields, or other open areas. The Bronze Copper is larger and prefers wet meadows, while the Dorcas Copper lives in more northern areas and different wetland types. The bog copper's exclusive relationship with cranberry plants sets it apart from both relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives, the Bronze Copper is the largest of New England's copper butterflies and shows the most pronounced metallic sheen.
